focus.note: Some verbs and adjectives need one small word after them. Learn the pair together, not the word alone.

tfn.s: The article suggests that the same evening can feel different from one week to the next.
tfn.why: The text says a week later "the identical empty evening feels flat and lonely" and that nothing in the room has changed.

tfn.s: The researchers found that reading about the benefits of being alone had no effect on beliefs.
tfn.why: The text says it "shifted people's beliefs in a positive direction".

tfn.s: The article says loneliness is only a misunderstanding.
tfn.why: The text says: "None of this means loneliness is a misunderstanding".

tfn.s: Most of the people in the daily-life studies were under thirty.
tfn.why: The text gives no information about the age of the people.

tfn.s: The study found a pattern across countries, but it cannot show which came first.
tfn.why: The text reports the same pattern across countries, and says the influence "may run both ways".

focus.note: Many nouns and adjectives take a fixed preposition, such as shortage of or to blame for. Learn the whole phrase.

speak.title: Role-play: a cancelled evening
speak.setup: Work in pairs. Read your card, then have the conversation. Swap roles and do it again.

a.role: the flatmate who wants a quiet night
a.text: Your friend cancelled your plans for tonight. You're delighted and want to stay in alone. Your flatmate wants company. Explain why time alone matters to you and suggest a fair compromise.

b.text: Your plans for tonight have fallen through and you feel a little lonely. Ask your flatmate to do something together. Explain why, and listen to their reasons.

phrases: I was really looking forward to a quiet night.
It's not that I don't like your company.
Could we do something together tomorrow instead?
I'd rather spend the evening on my own.
I don't want you to feel lonely.
How about a short walk and then I'm yours?
speak.after: Afterwards, tell the class: did you agree on a plan, and who gave way more?
